newsitem.title: MALTA: EU considering debt scheme for Mediterranean.
newsitem.headline: EU considering debt scheme for Mediterranean.

text.p: The European Union and 12 Mediterranean countries are considering the possibility of converting national debt owed to the EU into shareholder equity or direct investment capital.

A draft final declaration obtained by Reuters from a meeting of EU and 12 Mediterranean foreign ministers which began on Tuesday, says officials are considering the debt conversion plan in order to boost investment in the region.
The scheme is part of a three-tiered Euro-Med accord which seeks to boost political, economic and cultural links between the 15 EU nations and their southern Mediterranean neighbours.

"The participants underline the importance of ... studying the possibility of reducing the external indebtedness of the Mediterranean partner countries ... and its conversion into shareholdings or direct investments to compensate for the low level of European direct investments in partner countries," the declaration says.
The debt scheme is one of a number of points which had still not been finalised as ministers gathered for the opening of the conference.

Officials were still discussing the possibility of including a reference to "decision-making" in the final declaration, suggesting some want the Euro-Med partnership to expand from what is often considered just a forum for exchanging ideas.
The partnership, launched in Barcelona in November 1995, promises over 4.7 billion European Currency Units ($6.4 billion) in European grants, aid and soft loans up to the end of the century.
Other points still to be finalised include references to promoting democratic institutions and calling for adherance to international human rights standards.
The declaration concedes that the Middle East Peace crisis continues to overshadow EU-Mediterranean relations despite the efforts of the European Commission to concentrate on more technical aspects.

"(The participants) reiterate that this Euro-Mediterranean initiative is not intended to replace the other activities and initiatives undertaken in the interest of peace, stability and development in the region," it says. "But that it will contribute to ... the realisation of a just, comprehensive and lasting peace settlement in the Middle east....including the principle of land for peace, with all that this implies".

Officials of the European Commission -- the EU's executive -- say the maturity of the partnership can be demonstrated by the fact that Arab states have been prepared to participate despite the presence of Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.
Arab nations decided two weeks ago to sever formal links with Israel after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave the go- ahead for a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem.
On the political front, the declaration calls for increased cooperation on "preventative diplomacy, disarmament and arms control, drugs and organised crime and terrorism and democracy.

Economic aspects include a reiteration of efforts to turn the Euro-Med region into a free-trade zone by the year 2010 as well as calling for more cooperation on harmonising customs, standards and mutual recognition agreements.
